Avouch
a-VOWCH
verb
From the Old French avochier, “to call upon, to summon as witness,” from the Latin advocare, “to call to” (ad- + vocare, “to call”); hence to declare openly, to avow, to affirm a thing solemnly and publicly as one’s own.

Biblical Definition

To avouch is to declare a thing openly and bind oneself to the declaration — to avow before witnesses, calling others to hear what one owns. The word occurs only twice in all Scripture, side by side, and it carries the covenant formula of the Old Testament: “Thou hast avouched the LORD this day to be thy God, and to walk in his ways, and to keep his statutes… And the LORD hath avouched thee this day to be his peculiar people” (Deu 26:17-18). Here is the covenant in one breath, and it is mutual — He is ours and we are His — but it is not equal, and the order is everything. Israel avouches the LORD only because the LORD first avouched Israel; she does not create the bond by her declaration but confesses one that sovereign love had already made. Nor is the avouching a private sentiment. It is a public, spoken, binding word committing the whole life — to walk in His ways and hearken unto His voice — with the promise that God will “make thee high above all nations… and that thou mayest be an holy people unto the LORD thy God” (Deu 26:19). Peter carries the very phrase into the church: “ye are… a peculiar people; that ye should shew forth the praises of him who hath called you out of darkness into his marvellous light” (1Pe 2:9). God avouches first; His people answer.

Webster 1828 Definition

To declare openly; to avow; to affirm a thing solemnly and publicly as one’s own.

expand to see more

AVOUCH, to affirm openly; to declare; to avow; to maintain a thing as one’s own.

From the Latin advocare, “to call to,” through Old French avochier.

It denotes not a private opinion but a public, binding declaration.

Israel avouched the LORD to be her God (Deu 26:17).

The LORD avouched Israel to be His peculiar people (Deu 26:18).

Key Scripture

Deu 26:17 — "Thou hast avouched the LORD this day to be thy God, and to walk in his ways, and to keep his statutes, and his commandments, and his judgments, and to hearken unto his voice:"

Deu 26:18 — "And the LORD hath avouched thee this day to be his peculiar people, as he hath promised thee, and that thou shouldest keep all his commandments;"

Deu 26:19 — "And to make thee high above all nations which he hath made, in praise, and in name, and in honour; and that thou mayest be an holy people unto the LORD thy God, as he hath spoken."

1Pe 2:9 — "But ye are a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, an holy nation, a peculiar people; that ye should shew forth the praises of him who hath called you out of darkness into his marvellous light:"

Modern Corruption

Not a contested doctrine but the old covenant formula; it recovers that God avouched first, and that His covenant is no contract to be kept while convenient.

expand to see more

The word rebukes a religion of private and unspoken sentiment. To avouch is to say a thing out loud, before witnesses, and to be held to it — and the age much prefers a faith that commits to nothing it must name. It prefers, too, the contract to the covenant: an arrangement entered for benefit, weighed while it serves, and dissolved when it ceases to please. But Deuteronomy 26 is not a bargain struck between parties of equal standing; it is the LORD binding a people to Himself and that people answering with their whole life — to walk in His ways, to keep His statutes, to hearken unto His voice. Where the covenant is downgraded to a contract, the marriage vow follows it down, and so does church membership, for both were modelled on this.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the order of the two avouchings. Israel avouched the LORD to be her God; but the LORD avouched Israel to be His peculiar people, and He did it first. She did not make the covenant by confessing it; she confessed a covenant sovereign love had already made, for He did not set His love upon her because she was more in number than any people — she was the fewest of all — but because the LORD loved her. So the believer’s confession never creates his standing; it answers a God who chose him before the foundation of the world. We love him, because he first loved us; and we avouch Him, because He first avouched us.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The word means to declare openly and bind oneself to the declaration, to avow publicly.

expand to see more

Avouch — Old French avochier, from Latin advocare, “to call to.”

It denotes an open, public, binding declaration, not a private sentiment.

It occurs but twice in Scripture, in the covenant formula of Deu 26:17-18.

Israel avouched the LORD to be her God, and He avouched her His people.

God avouches first; the confession of His people is the answer.

Usage

"Thou hast avouched the LORD this day to be thy God — a public word, not a private mood."

"The LORD hath avouched thee to be his peculiar people: He owns His own out loud."

"God avouched first; our confession does not make the covenant but answers it."
